name: crewAI

facts.description: Framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents. By fostering collaborative intelligence, CrewAI empowers agents to work together seamlessly, tackling complex tasks.

title: CrewAI: A Python Framework for Orchestrating Multi-Agent AI Workflows
answer: CrewAI is an open-source Python framework, made by CrewAI Inc. and released under the MIT licence, for orchestrating role-playing autonomous AI agents that collaborate on multi-step tasks. It sits in the orchestration layer of the AI stack, above the language models and tools that agents call. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that its production story rests on Flows, a thin deterministic code layer, alongside the more open-ended crews, so the framework spans quick prototypes and governed deployments rather than being only one or the other.

sections.body: CrewAI is a framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents, built and maintained by CrewAI Inc. and distributed under the MIT licence. Its repository, crewAIInc/crewAI, is written in Python and had its most recent push on 3 October 2026, with roughly 59,000 stars at the time of writing. The official site describes it as an open-source framework for building and orchestrating multi-agent AI workflows, in which developers define autonomous agents with specific roles, goals and backstories that can use tools, process tasks and interact with one another. It is powered by language models, so it does not train or serve models itself. It occupies the orchestration layer of the AI stack, sitting above model providers and tools and below the application, and it is used to coordinate several agents rather than to replace a single model call.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs CrewAI handles are multi-step, language-heavy automations: research, analysis, drafting and review carried out by collaborating agents, with tool calls and API calls along the way. The site's own tutorial builds a researcher agent that searches the web through SerperDevTool and produces a report, and its NVIDIA page describes agents that automatically write project documentation. The framework is strongest where a task needs reasoning over unstructured data and dynamic decomposition rather than a fixed script. The site contrasts it with enterprise RPA platforms, noting that many enterprises use RPA for deterministic UI workflows and CrewAI for cognitive, language-heavy automations, and it recommends CrewAI when tasks require reasoning, unstructured data, tool calls and collaborating agents. Its production path adds tracing, guardrails and an Agent Management Platform, and the NVIDIA integration lets agents be powered by models hosted on NVIDIA NIM microservices.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: CrewAI is a Python framework, so working Python is the first prerequisite, and the site's tutorial assumes a developer who can install packages, manage an API key in a .env file and run a script. The core vocabulary is small and is explained directly on the site: an agent is defined by role, goal and backstory, a task is a unit of work assigned to an agent with a description and an expected output, a crew is a collection of agents and tasks, and a process such as Process.sequential sets the execution order. No mathematics beyond ordinary programming is implied by the material, and no systems knowledge is required to start, though production use brings in tracing, guardrails and cost control. For a beginner the official site offers a developer portal, a step-by-step tutorial with complete code in a GitHub repository, an MCP server and an llms-full.txt file intended to make the documentation readable by agents themselves.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around CrewAI includes the crewai and crewai-tools packages installed in the site's own tutorial, integrations with model providers such as Cerebras and with NVIDIA NIM microservices as part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise, and a comparison page that places it beside Microsoft Agent Framework, Automation Anywhere, AutoGen and MetaGPT. The site points to a developer portal, an MCP server and llms-full.txt as agent-ready documentation, and to a GitHub repository holding the tutorial code. Community scale is suggested by the repository's roughly 59,000 stars and by the site's claim of 40,000 GitHub stars at the time of its NVIDIA announcement, a figure that has since grown. The site also publishes survey reports, including one based on 500 executives and another drawing on over 4,500 professionals building AI agents, which function as community-facing material.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: CrewAI is presented as serving both ends. A crew of agents with roles, goals and backstories can be defined in a short script and started with kickoff(), which is the prototyping path shown in the Cerebras tutorial. For production, the site's architecture article argues that the gap in agentic AI is not intelligence but architecture, and describes Agentic Systems that pair a deterministic backbone called Flows with intelligence deployed where it matters. Flows are described as a very thin code layer with almost no abstractions, just flexible decorators and state management, handling conditional branching, state across steps and custom business logic, with the same inputs producing the same execution path. The cost of this split is that developers must decide where determinism ends and agency begins, and the site warns against both heavy scaffolding that cannot adapt and unbounded agency without architectural constraints.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site's claims about adoption are substantial: 1.4 billion agentic automations, 60 percent of the Fortune 500, production use cases at PwC and the startup Parloa, and a survey in which 81 percent of large enterprises say they have fully adopted or are actively scaling agentic AI. It also reports that 57 percent of organizations prefer building on existing open-source tools rather than starting from scratch, which favors a framework like this one. These figures come from CrewAI's own marketing and survey material and are not independently verified here. On the question of whether it is a current standard or a legacy choice, the facts and the site support only that it is actively developed, widely starred and positioned as a current option, not that it has displaced any particular alternative. For someone choosing what to learn, that means CrewAI is a reasonable bet in the multi-agent orchestration space, with the caveat that the space itself is young and the site's adoption numbers are self-reported.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: CrewAI is Python-first, and the site describes it as an open, Python-first multi-agent framework, which places it naturally beside Python model clients, tool libraries and data stacks. It is model-agnostic in practice: the tutorial wires it to Cerebras-hosted Llama models, the NVIDIA page wires it to models on NVIDIA NIM, and the site's cost article discusses choosing among Opus, GPT-4o, Gemini Pro, Haiku and 4o-mini for different tasks. It is typically compared with Microsoft Agent Framework, which targets .NET and Azure ecosystems, and with Automation Anywhere for enterprise RPA, and the site suggests choosing CrewAI for open Python-first crews and Microsoft Agent Framework when standardizing on Azure AI services. The polyglot pattern it belongs to is one where orchestration lives in Python while models are served elsewhere, whether on a provider's API, on NVIDIA hardware or on custom inference like Cerebras's Wafer Scale Engine 3.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid about several weaknesses. It warns that most agentic implementations are either too rigid or too loose, that prompt chains passing as agents and graph structures chosen for maintainability are common mistakes, and that token spend can explode: a ten-step agent run with a 30,000-token prompt can reach 500,000 to 2 million tokens, and the site estimates that 60 to 80 percent of enterprise token spend goes to use cases that have not proven business value. It also reports that data readiness and integration challenges, cited by 35 percent of respondents, and insufficient talent or skills, cited by 33 percent, are the top obstacles to adoption. What the official material does not settle is how much of the reported adoption is deep production use rather than pilots, how the framework performs against alternatives on identical workloads, and how stable its APIs will remain as the project evolves. Those questions are left open by the pages read.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
